questions.q: A researcher re-runs an unchanged backtest script six months later and gets a different Sharpe ratio. According to this lesson, what is the most likely cause?
options: Python's floating-point arithmetic changed between versions
The underlying data changed (e.g. restated fundamentals or a new data pull) even though the code and git history show nothing different
Git automatically modifies old commits over time
pandas randomizes row order on every import
questions.explain: The code and parameters can be byte-identical to last time while the input data silently changed underneath -- a restated value, an updated table, a different pull -- which is exactly the failure mode this lesson addresses with data versioning.

questions.q: In experiment tracking (e.g. the MLflow-style pattern), what are the three things logged per run?
options: Parameters, metrics, and artifacts
Only the final Sharpe ratio
The git commit hash and nothing else
CPU usage, memory usage, and disk usage
questions.explain: Experiment tracking logs the input parameters that varied (e.g. lookback window), the resulting metrics (e.g. Sharpe ratio), and any output artifacts (e.g. a plot or results table), making every run queryable later.

questions.q: What does content-addressed storage (the approach tools like DVC use) provide that simply hashing a file does not?
options: It makes the dataset load faster at runtime
It automatically fixes data errors before storage
It stores large data files by their content hash and ties that storage to git, so checking out an old commit retrieves the exact dataset that commit was built against
It encrypts data at rest for compliance purposes
questions.explain: Content-addressed storage extends git-style versioning to data too large to put directly in git, linking a specific git commit to the exact data snapshot it was built against -- a hash alone tells you data changed, but doesn't manage retrieving old versions.

questions.q: In the `fingerprint` example, why does hashing `df.to_csv(index=False)` rather than the DataFrame object directly matter?
options: to_csv() is required because hashlib cannot hash DataFrames
It produces a stable byte representation of the data's actual contents that can be hashed consistently and compared across runs
It compresses the DataFrame to save disk space
It removes duplicate rows before hashing
questions.explain: hashlib operates on bytes, not Python objects, so the DataFrame needs a stable byte representation first; to_csv(index=False) gives a consistent serialization of the actual values, which is what SHA-256 then hashes.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, changing a single close price from 191.04 to 191.50 changed the SHA-256 fingerprint completely rather than slightly. Why is that the desired property?
options: It proves the hash function is broken and should not be used
It guarantees the fingerprint can't accidentally match two datasets that differ, even by one value, which is exactly what's needed to detect a silent restatement
It means the data was corrupted during hashing
SHA-256 only works correctly on numeric columns
questions.explain: Cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 are designed so any change to the input, however small, produces an unrelated-looking output -- this is what makes the fingerprint reliable for detecting that data changed at all, rather than by how much.
